extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method, induction, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: General principles and standards for observing, experimenting, and inferring causal laws in scientific/inductive inquiry. Covers when causes compose additively, when new laws emerge, and how observation and experiment must be conducted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the Composition of Causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The joint effect of several causes is identical with the sum of their separate effects; in such cases the same law which expresses the effect of each cause acting alone also correctly expresses the part due to that cause when combined with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplified in mechanics (composition of forces: north + east forces produce movement equal to each separately). Where this principle holds, one can often deduce the result of combined causes a priori from the laws governing each separately; this is the basis for deductive treatment in mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence of heteropathic combinations (new laws arise)
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases (notably chemical combinations and organized bodies) the joint action of causes produces effects heterogeneous to those produced by each cause separately; new properties and laws appear which are not the sum of component effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: water's properties are not traceable to hydrogen or oxygen alone; taste of sugar of lead is not the sum of its ingredients. Such cases prevent straightforward deduction from ingredient laws and require direct experiment to discover new laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish when composition applies versus when new laws govern
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the same law that governs each cause separately continues to operate when causes act together, or whether their conjunction calls into action different laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical phenomena typically obey composition; chemical and biological phenomena often do not. Correct identification dictates whether predictive/deductive methods apply or whether specific experiments for the combination are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experiment to separate facts in nature (experimental isolation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental analysis (partitioning phenomena conceptually) is necessary but insufficient; to assign which antecedents are invariably attendant on which consequents one must attempt to separate facts from one another in nature by experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First do the intellectual decomposition, then perform experiments that isolate causes. Observation alone without experimental separation will not reliably establish causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of careful observational decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The observer must decompose complex appearances into their constituent facts; good observation is not mere seeing but seeing the parts of a thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varieties of faulty observation are listed: inattention (overlooking facts), confusing seen with imagined or inferred, noting kinds without quantities, or making a poor partition of parts. Training and disposition influence observational quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every fact that begins to exist has a proximate cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Every fact which begins to exist has a cause found among the facts that immediately preceded its occurrence; the present is the infallible result of past facts, more immediately of the facts at the previous moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle motivates resolving complex antecedents into simpler antecedents to find which part produces each consequent; it underpins causal inquiry and the analytical operation of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of effects to causes is conditional
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom that effects are proportional to their causes holds only as a particular case of the Composition of Causes; it applies when causes are homogeneous and composition holds, but fails where augmentation of a cause changes the kind of effect produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: increasing heat may cause expansion, then melting, then decomposition — qualitatively different effects that defy a simple proportional law. Recognize limits of proportionality reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariant properties may persist under combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain properties (e.g., weight) remain additive and obey the same laws in all combinations; such invariants can be relied upon across compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight of a compound equals sum of weights of its elements; mechanical and chemical properties of parts may persist so long as they are not counteracted by new laws arising from organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heteropathic laws can themselves be composed (higher-level deduction possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws generated by combinations (heteropathic laws) may themselves compose with each other and with original laws, making it possible that chemistry and physiology could become more deductive as higher-level regularities are discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and partial generalizations: Dalton's law of definite proportions, Berthollet's observations on salt decomposition, law of isomorphism. Seek regularities linking compound properties to elements to enable broader deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction's chief objective: ascertain laws of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The main business of induction is to determine which causes are correctly assigned to which effects, and vice versa, so as to explain uniformities and predict events given requisite data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction is essentially inquiry into cases of causation; success enables explanation of uniformities and prediction of individual facts when antecedent circumstances are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing from a singular kind of phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not infer that a singular or peculiar phenomenon (e.g., volition as observed in humans) is the origin of all other phenomena without adequate grounds; analogies must be tested by conformity of laws, not assumed universal from a single class of cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes inferring universal causal principles from the special case of human volition. Historical examples (Thales, Anaximenes, Cartesians, Leibnitz) show divergent views; do not rely on the mere inconceivability of alternatives as proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize thresholds where augmentation alters kind of effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When increasing the quantity or intensity of a cause, be alert for qualitative transitions where the nature of the effect changes and previous laws (including proportionality) cease to apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by heat causing expansion at one level, melting at another, decomposition at a higher level; such thresholds mark failure of simple additive or proportional reasoning and require new analysis/experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational skill is cultivated by mental preparation (rules of self-education)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no direct Art of Observing that teaches observation mechanically; rather, there are rules for preparing one's mind—modes of mental culture—that make a person capable of good observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between logical rules (inductive method) and educational rules (training intellect and sensibilities). Instruction should aim to put the observer into a state most fitted to observe or invent.
